cards.front: {{c1::Oncotic pressure}} is the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins, drawing water toward the side with more protein.
cards.quote: Oncotic pressure is the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins, drawing water toward the side with more protein.

cards.front: The {{c1::glycocalyx}} is a coat of proteoglycans and glycoproteins lining every capillary, its fibres covering the openings between and through the endothelial cells.
cards.back: In the revised Starling model it acts as the sieve that holds plasma protein back.
cards.quote: The glycocalyx is a coat of proteoglycans and glycoproteins (sugar-covered proteins) lining every capillary, its fibres covering the openings between and through the cells.

cards.front: By the revised Starling principle, why can plasma protein slow capillary filtration but not reverse it for long?
cards.back: Filtering rinses protein from under the glycocalyx and keeps the hold-back strong. Absorbing leaves protein behind there and weakens the hold-back, so absorption switches itself off (the no-absorption rule).
cards.quote: So plasma protein can slow filtration but cannot reverse it for long (the no-absorption rule).

cards.front: Name the situations the no-absorption rule of capillary exchange does not cover.
cards.back: The moments after a sudden fall in pressure, the few beds that absorb steadily, sinusoids, and the glomerulus (its own balance).
cards.quote: It does not cover the moments after a sudden fall in pressure, the few beds that absorb steadily, sinusoids, or the glomerulus (its own balance).

cards.front: In capillary exchange, what is the 'push', and what is it in resting skeletal muscle with Pc = 18 mmHg and Pi = -1 mmHg?
cards.back: Pc - Pi, capillary pressure minus tissue pressure: 18 - (-1) = 19 mmHg.
cards.quote: The push is the pressure inside the capillary, Pc, minus the pressure in the tissue, Pi.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: Why does a rise in venous pressure raise capillary pressure (Pc) more than an equal rise in arterial pressure?
cards.back: Pc sits between arterial and venous pressure, placed by the ratio of pre- to postcapillary resistance, and that ratio puts it nearer the venous side.
cards.quote: so a rise in venous pressure moves it more than an equal rise in arterial pressure.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: What is interstitial pressure (Pi) in loose tissues such as skin, and how does a rise in Pi affect filtration?
cards.back: Slightly below atmospheric, about -1 mmHg (positive in some organs such as liver and kidney). A rise in Pi opposes filtration.
cards.quote: Pi is slightly below atmospheric in loose tissues such as skin, intestine and lung, about -1 mmHg, though positive in some organs such as liver and kidney.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: Plasma oncotic pressure is about 26 mmHg in adults by one review, and {{c1::albumin}} supplies most of it, about 65 to 80 percent by different reviews.
cards.back: Globulins supply the rest.
cards.quote: Albumin supplies most of it, about 65 to 80 percent by different reviews, and globulins supply the rest.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: What is the reflection coefficient, sigma, and about what is it for albumin across capillary walls?
cards.back: The fraction of a solute's full oncotic pull it exerts across the wall: 1 if the wall passes water and no solute, 0 if it hinders the solute no more than water. For albumin about 0.8 to 0.96 in the single vessels and tissues measured, varying with tissue; take 0.9.
cards.quote: For albumin it is high, about 0.8 to 0.96 in the single vessels and tissues measured, varying with the tissue; take 0.9.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: For whole tissues, hydraulic conductivity Lp times wall area S is the {{c1::filtration coefficient}}, Kf.
cards.back: It sets how much water flow each mmHg of net pressure buys.
cards.quote: The conductance is the hydraulic conductivity, Lp, times the wall area, S; for whole tissues their product is the filtration coefficient, Kf.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: Arterial end of a muscle capillary: Pc = 32, Pi = -1, pi_p = 26, pi_g = 6 (all mmHg), sigma = 0.9. What is the net filtration pressure?
cards.back: Push = 32 - (-1) = 33 mmHg. Hold-back = 0.9 x (26 - 6) = 18 mmHg. Net = 33 - 18 = +15 mmHg, outward (filtration).
cards.quote: Push 33 mmHg, hold-back 18 mmHg, net +15 mmHg outward.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: Resting muscle: Pc = 18, Pi = -1, pi_p = 26, pi_g = 6 (mmHg). Inflammation lowers sigma for albumin from 0.9 to 0.6, other values unchanged. How does net filtration pressure change?
cards.back: Push = 19 mmHg. Before: hold-back 0.9 x 20 = 18, net +1 mmHg. After: hold-back 0.6 x 20 = 12, net +7 mmHg outward, seven times higher.
cards.why: A protein can pull water back only across a wall it cannot easily cross; lower sigma means a weaker hold-back.
cards.quote: A protein can only pull water back across a wall it cannot easily cross.
cards.section: Push, hold-back and conductance

cards.front: Which capillary type lines (a) skeletal muscle, skin and lung, (b) intestinal villi and renal peritubular capillaries, (c) liver, spleen and bone marrow?
cards.back: (a) Continuous, (b) fenestrated, (c) sinusoidal. Fenestrated vessels pass more water and small solute than continuous ones; sinusoids hold back large molecules little.
cards.quote: Fenestrated capillaries (intestinal villi, renal peritubular capillaries, endocrine glands) add fenestrae, pores through the thinnest parts of the cell, here covered by a thin diaphragm.
cards.section: Why sigma differs from bed to bed

cards.front: How does glucose cross the capillary wall in skeletal muscle, and how does that differ in brain?
cards.back: In muscle it diffuses through the intercellular clefts. Brain capillaries close that route, so glucose crosses them on transporters.
cards.quote: brain capillaries close this route, and glucose crosses them on transporters.
cards.section: Why sigma differs from bed to bed

cards.front: For oxygen and small solutes such as glucose, which moves more across a capillary wall: diffusion or the water carried by filtration? By what route does oxygen cross?
cards.back: Diffusion, by far. Oxygen and other lipid-soluble molecules diffuse through the endothelial membranes over the whole surface.
cards.quote: For them, diffusion moves far more across the wall than filtering water carries.
cards.section: Why sigma differs from bed to bed

cards.front: A muscle venule is held at low pressure, so with tissue-side protein fixed the forces favour absorption. Predict what happens to absorption over time, and why.
cards.back: It absorbs only briefly. Water leaves the film under the glycocalyx for the plasma and protein is left behind, so pi_g climbs until the hold-back falls to match the push; absorption stops.
cards.quote: Water leaves the film for the plasma and protein is left behind, so pi_g climbs until the hold-back falls to match the push.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: In a filtering capillary, why does the subglycocalyx oncotic pressure (pi_g) stay below the average interstitial oncotic pressure?
cards.back: Nearly protein-free filtrate streams out along the cleft and rinses the film. Protein arriving by large pores must diffuse back against this stream. Faster filtration rinses harder.
cards.quote: When the vessel filters, nearly protein-free fluid streams out along the cleft, rinsing the film.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: Why is there no true Starling equilibrium (zero fluid movement with a stable protein difference) across a capillary wall?
cards.back: If water stopped moving, protein would diffuse out until the protein difference across the glycocalyx vanished.
cards.quote: If water stopped moving, protein would diffuse out until the difference vanished.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: Describe the hockey-stick curve of steady filtration against capillary pressure.
cards.back: Above a bend where the push nears sigma x pi_p (about 23 mmHg), filtration rises steeply, nearly linearly. Below it, filtrate is too slow to wash protein away, so the curve flattens toward zero but stays positive.
cards.why: The old diagram is the straight line continued below zero.
cards.quote: Below it the filtrate is too slow to wash protein away, so the curve flattens toward zero but stays positive.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: What is autotransfusion after blood loss, and why is it temporary?
cards.back: A sudden fall in capillary pressure makes vessels absorb tissue fluid into the blood. It lasts until protein builds up under the glycocalyx; then the vessel filters slightly again.
cards.quote: After a sudden fall in capillary pressure, as after blood loss, a vessel absorbs until protein builds up under the glycocalyx, then filters slightly again.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: Which microvascular beds absorb fluid steadily, and what makes that possible?
cards.back: Intestinal mucosa and renal peritubular capillaries, where an epithelium delivers nearly protein-free fluid, and lymph nodes, where incoming lymph is lower in protein than plasma. A second stream keeps the tissue side rinsed.
cards.quote: And steady absorption needs a second stream that keeps the tissue side rinsed with protein-poor fluid.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: A single frog mesenteric capillary is perfused through a micropipette and held at low pressure. What was seen, and what does it show?
cards.back: It absorbed only briefly; in the steady state fluid movement fell to near zero or slight filtration. Absorption switches itself off, against the venous-end reabsorption model.
cards.quote: a vessel held at low pressure absorbed only briefly; in the steady state, fluid movement fell to near zero or slight filtration.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: If the glycocalyx is the sieve (rat and frog mesentery evidence), an enzyme strips part of it in a muscle bed. Predict the effect on Lp, sigma for albumin, steady filtration, and the protein content of the lymph.
cards.back: Lp rises and sigma falls, so filtration rises through both a larger conductance and a weaker hold-back. More albumin escapes, so lymph protein stays high, a permeability pattern.
cards.why: Rests on the glycocalyx being the sieve and on sigma scaling the hold-back.
cards.quote: When enzymes strip part of the glycocalyx, the same vessel becomes leakier to water and albumin.
cards.section: Why the venous end does not reabsorb

cards.front: How does filtrate enter the initial lymphatics?
cards.back: Initial lymphatics are blind-ended; their overlapping cells meet at discontinuous button junctions, and flap-like openings between the buttons act as primary valves.
cards.quote: Filtrate enters blind-ended initial lymphatics, whose overlapping cells meet at discontinuous button junctions, with flap-like openings between the buttons acting as the primary valves.
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: Collecting lymphatics have secondary valves, and each segment between two of them is a {{c1::lymphangion}}, a contractile pump.
cards.back: Lymph moves by this intrinsic pumping plus extrinsic squeezing from muscle and breathing.
cards.quote: Collecting lymphatics have secondary valves, and each segment between two of them is a lymphangion, a contractile pump.
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: Why must lymph carry plasma protein away from a tissue, not just water?
cards.back: Protein leaks through the large pores. Without removal it would build up in the tissue, shrink the protein difference across the wall, and the hold-back would fail.
cards.quote: They must also carry the plasma protein that leaked through the large pores, or protein would build up in the tissue and the hold-back would fail.
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: The thoracic duct enters the veins at the junction of the {{c1::left subclavian and left internal jugular}} veins.
cards.back: The right lymphatic duct drains on the right.
cards.quote: The rest enters the veins by the thoracic duct, at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: What probably drives lymph flow in lymphatics running inside skeletal muscle, and why?
cards.back: Muscle contraction, because these lymphatics are reported to have little or no smooth muscle of their own.
cards.quote: Lymphatics running inside skeletal muscle are reported to have little or no smooth muscle, so muscle contraction probably drives flow there.
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: The thoracic duct is blocked. A meal contains long-chain and medium-chain fatty acids. Which is mainly kept from reaching the blood, and why?
cards.back: Long-chain fat. It leaves intestinal cells as chylomicrons, enters the lacteals and reaches blood through the thoracic duct. Medium-chain fatty acids go mostly by the portal vein.
cards.quote: Medium-chain fatty acids go mostly by the portal vein.
cards.section: Where the fluid goes: lymph

cards.front: Resting adult muscle, 10 kg: Kf = 0.005 mL per min per mmHg per 100 g, Pc = 18, Pi = -1, pi_p = 26, pi_g = 6 (mmHg), sigma = 0.9. What is the filtration rate, per minute and per day?
cards.back: Net = 19 - 0.9 x 20 = +1 mmHg. Jv = 0.005 x 1 x 100 = 0.5 mL per min, or 720 mL per day, returned as lymph.
cards.quote: Jv = 0.005 x 1 x 100 = 0.5 mL per min, or 720 mL per day, returned as lymph.
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle, three states

cards.front: In heart failure, the same 10 kg muscle (Kf 0.005 mL per min per mmHg per 100 g, sigma 0.9, pi_p 26 mmHg) settles at Pc = 28, Pi = +2, pi_g = 3 mmHg. Lymph can carry at most 1.5 mL per min. Does the muscle swell?
cards.back: Net = (28 - 2) - 0.9 x (26 - 3) = 5.3 mmHg; Jv = 0.005 x 5.3 x 100 = 2.65 mL per min. Excess 1.15 mL per min, about 1.7 L a day: edema.
cards.quote: Filtration of 2.65 mL per min beats a lymph ceiling of 1.5 mL per min by 1.15 mL per min, about 1.7 L a day: edema.
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle, three states

cards.front: Blood loss lowers Pc to 10 mmHg in the 10 kg muscle (Pi -1, pi_p 26, pi_g 6 mmHg, sigma 0.9, Kf 0.005 mL per min per mmHg per 100 g). What is the initial fluid movement, and at what pi_g does it stop?
cards.back: Net = 11 - 18 = -7 mmHg: absorption of 3.5 mL per min at first. It stops when 0.9 x (26 - pi_g) = 11, at pi_g = 13.8 mmHg; then slight filtration resumes.
cards.quote: It stops when 0.9 x (26 - pi_g) = 11, at pi_g = 13.8 mmHg, and then the vessel goes back to filtering slightly
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle, three states

cards.front: Name the three safety factors that limit edema.
cards.back: Interstitial pressure (Pi) rises as fluid collects; washout, as faster filtration rinses away tissue and subglycocalyx protein; and lymph flow rises.
cards.quote: Three safety factors limit swelling: Pi rises as fluid collects, washout (protein rinsed away by faster filtration) lowers tissue and subglycocalyx protein, and lymph flow rises.
cards.section: Four ways to make edema, and what holds it back

cards.front: Name the four routes to edema and the term each mainly changes.
cards.back: Raised capillary pressure (push rises); low plasma protein (pi_p falls); leaky microvessels (sigma falls); blocked lymph (drainage fails, tissue protein may build up).
cards.quote: Each cause moves mainly one term of the equation, or the lymph.
cards.section: Four ways to make edema, and what holds it back

cards.front: Two limbs are equally swollen: one from blocked lymphatics, one from raised venous pressure with intact lymph. Which has the higher interstitial protein, and why?
cards.back: The lymph-blocked limb. Leaked protein cannot leave, so it builds up and shrinks the hold-back. With raised venous pressure, faster filtration washes protein out and lymph removes it.
cards.why: Rests on lymph carrying protein away and the washout safety factor.
cards.quote: Edema is interstitial fluid accumulation when filtration exceeds lymph drainage.
cards.section: Four ways to make edema, and what holds it back

cards.front: In invented illustrative data from a dog paw prenodal lymphatic, lymph rises fivefold both with raised venous pressure and with histamine. Lymph-to-plasma protein ratio (L/P): baseline 0.5, venous pressure 0.25, histamine 0.7. What distinguishes the causes, and why is flow alone not enough?
cards.back: L/P. Pressure: water flow rises more than protein flow, so L/P falls (sieving, washout). Histamine opens venular gaps and lowers sigma, so L/P stays high. Histamine also raises Pc, so flow rises in both.
cards.quote: Histamine also dilates arterioles and raises Pc, so the rise in lymph flow alone does not separate the two causes; the high L/P is what points to permeability.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Plasma protein is 60 g per L. Lymph flow: baseline 0.05 mL per min at L/P 0.5; after histamine 0.25 mL per min at L/P 0.7. Calculate protein flux in each state.
cards.back: Flux = lymph flow x lymph protein. Baseline 0.05 x 30 mg per mL = 1.5 mg per min. Histamine 0.25 x 42 = 10.5 mg per min, seven times baseline.
cards.quote: histamine 0.25 x 42 = 10.5 mg per min, seven times baseline.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Resting muscle (push 19 mmHg, sigma 0.9): plasma oncotic pressure falls from 26 to 14 mmHg. Calculate net filtration pressure with pi_g fixed at 6 mmHg, then after washout lowers pi_g to 2 mmHg.
cards.back: pi_g 6: 19 - 0.9 x (14 - 6) = 11.8 mmHg (from +1). pi_g 2: 19 - 0.9 x 12 = 8.2 mmHg. Lower, but still large.
cards.quote: Washout lowers pi_g: at 2 mmHg, net = 19 - 0.9 x 12 = 8.2 mmHg.
cards.section: Back to the opening: life without albumin

cards.front: Adults with congenital analbuminemia have almost no plasma albumin, yet edema is usually mild. Explain.
cards.back: Filtration does rise, but the three safety factors act together: Pi rises, washout lowers tissue and subglycocalyx protein, and lymph flow rises. Globulins may partly stand in for albumin.
cards.quote: That may be why edema in congenital analbuminemia is common but usually mild, and a few people have none.
cards.section: Back to the opening: life without albumin

cards.front: Plasma oncotic pressure is raised by infusing albumin in a person whose muscle capillaries filter slightly. Predict steady fluid movement across those capillaries.
cards.back: Steady filtration slows but does not reverse. Any absorption would leave protein under the glycocalyx, raise pi_g and switch itself off (the no-absorption rule).
cards.quote: By the same rule, raising plasma oncotic pressure can slow steady filtration but not reverse it.
cards.section: Back to the opening: life without albumin

cards.front: If the glycocalyx is the sieve, what should neuraminidase do in single perfused rat mesenteric microvessels, what was found, and what are the limits?
cards.back: Predicted: Lp up, sigma down in the same vessel. Found: Lp rose 1.9-fold (1.39 to 2.68 x 10^-7 cm per s per cmH2O), sigma 0.96 to 0.87. Limits: rat only, enzyme may act beyond the glycocalyx.
cards.quote: Lp rose 1.9-fold, from 1.39 to 2.68 x 10^-7 cm per s per cmH2O, and sigma for albumin fell from 0.96 to 0.87.
cards.section: Testing the sieve

cards.front: A single microvessel is perfused with albumin solution of oncotic pressure 30 cmH2O; outside pressures are 0. Filtration falls to zero at 27 cmH2O. After an enzyme, the slope is unchanged and zero is at 21 cmH2O. Find sigma before and after, and interpret.
cards.back: Filtration = Lp x (P - sigma x 30). Before: sigma = 27 / 30 = 0.9. After: 21 / 30 = 0.7. Unchanged slope means Lp unchanged; only the albumin barrier fell.
cards.quote: measured Lp by Landis-Michel occlusion (the slope of filtration against pressure)
cards.section: Testing the sieve

cards.front: Histamine is injected under the scrotal skin of a rat, with a particulate tracer in the blood, and cremaster vessels are examined by electron microscopy. Where did the leak occur in this tissue?
cards.back: Gaps of about 0.1 to 0.8 micrometres opened between endothelial cells in venular-sized vessels; capillaries looked intact. The leak was in venules, between cells.
cards.quote: That located this leak in venules, between cells, and ruled out capillaries as its site in this tissue.
cards.section: Where an inflammatory leak happens
